recent_reports.title: Living Standards, Poverty and Inequality in the UK: 2024
recent_reports.summary: Comprehensive annual report on UK living standards. Covers the cost-of-living crisis impact on households, absolute and relative poverty trends, and the disproportionate effect of inflation on lower-income households who spend more on food and energy.
key_recommendations: Housing costs must be included in poverty measurement as they disproportionately affect low-income households.
Mortgage interest rate rises have had materially different effects across households — policy responses should be targeted accordingly.
Rising in-work poverty is driven by structural factors, not just wage levels — benefits architecture needs reform.
Material deprivation measures should sit alongside income-based poverty measures for a fuller picture.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: Partial — IFS confirms housing costs are central to poverty measurement, aligning with Fudge's housing-as-root-cause thesis. IFS is more cautious on structural interventions.

recent_reports.title: Economic Outlook: Navigating Narrow Paths
recent_reports.summary: IFS Green Budget chapter assessing UK economic prospects. UK GDP grew 0.9% in H1 2025, ahead of OBR expectations, but private domestic demand remains weak. Real GDP per capita grew just 0.1% in 2024. Business investment at 10.8% of GDP is well below US (16%) and Germany (17%) levels.
key_recommendations: Productivity is the most important determinant of the UK's longer-term economic outlook — must be the central policy focus.
Business investment at 10.8% of GDP remains well below US (16%) and Germany (17%) levels — structural gap requires policy response.
Fiscal consolidation must not crowd out the investment needed for long-run growth.
Real income growth expected to average 1.1% per year over the next five years — insufficient to close the living standards gap.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: High — directly supports Fudge's reindustrialisation thesis and critique of chronic UK underinvestment. IFS figures on business investment gap underpin his Pillar Two case.

recent_reports.title: Risks and Challenges for the Public Finances
recent_reports.summary: Detailed analysis of UK fiscal risks. Debt interest payments now exceed 4% of national income — highest since 1950 — and are expected to remain between 3.5–4% of GDP throughout the forecast horizon. This represents £64bn more than expected just three years ago, roughly equivalent to the entire schools budget.
key_recommendations: The five-year OBR forecast horizon creates structural bias against policies with long-term benefits — horizon should be extended.
OBR should publish long-term estimates of policies whose benefits or costs materialise beyond year five.
Current fiscal rules risk penalising productive investment — reform needed to distinguish current spending from capital investment.
Debt interest costs represent a permanent constraint on public service spending that must be honestly acknowledged.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: High — IFS analysis of fiscal rule design directly supports Fudge's argument that borrowing to invest in productive assets produces better long-run debt trajectory than austerity.

recent_reports.title: Options for Tax Increases
recent_reports.summary: Comprehensive assessment of tax reform options available to the UK government. Argues for alignment of tax rates across all forms of income and gains to remove distortions. Stamp duty identified as one of the UK's most damaging taxes. Closing the corporation tax gap is a significant untapped revenue source.
key_recommendations: Overall tax rates should be aligned across all forms of income and gains — current differential rates distort investment decisions.
Capital gains tax reform must fix the tax base (removing forgiveness at death, treating losses more generously) before adjusting rates.
Stamp duty is among the worst and most damaging UK taxes — should be reformed or replaced.
Closing the corporation tax gap (53% of small businesses under-declared 2021-22) is a significant untapped revenue source.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: Partial — IFS supports tax base reform broadly. Fudge proposes zero CGT on productive investment, which IFS would assess as creating new distortions. IFS more cautious on property tax reform speed.

recent_reports.title: Challenging Inequalities (IFS Deaton Review — Final Publication)
recent_reports.summary: Final output of the multi-year IFS Deaton Review of inequalities. Summarises the breadth of UK inequalities across income, health, geography, and political power. Finds persistent economic stagnation accompanied by declining institutional trust. Political capture of policy by asset-owning classes identified as a root cause of failure to address economic inequality.
key_recommendations: Inequalities in the UK are interconnected — policymakers must address them systemically, not in silos.
Geographical inequality is deeply structural and requires sustained place-based industrial policy — not just redistribution.
Health inequalities have direct economic consequences through inactivity — NHS investment is economic policy, not just social spending.
Political inequality (capture of policy by asset-owning classes) is a root cause of failure to address economic inequality.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: High — the Deaton Review's finding that political inequality (property-owning MPs) structurally prevents reform is central to Fudge's diagnosis. His conduct and register of interests reforms directly address this.

Will planning reform make housing more affordable?
recent_reports.summary: Will planning reform make housing more affordable? Far too many people lack an affordable, safe, secure, decent place to call home. Far too many homes are disconnected from the spaces and services that make the economy tick and allow communities to thrive: public transport, working doctors' surgeries, parks and playgrounds, shops and pubs.
key_recommendations: Housing costs push over one million children into poverty All this points to a deep perversity in housing policy: increasing market supply is supposed to improve affordability, but that could only happen now by bringing down prices, which would hurt the 7.5 million households who have already taken out a mortgage.

In the dash to deliver as many units as possible, policy-makers risk forgetting what they were trying to do in the first place: make sure people have good quality, affordable, secure homes in places where they want to live.
Instead, the government has proposed reducing or delaying requirements to provide social and affordable homes through the planning system.

recent_reports.title: Rethinking public sector productivity
recent_reports.summary: This project is funded by the Robertson Trust. The Spending Review published alongside the 2026-27 Budget commits the Scottish government to a programme of reform ‘designed to protect frontline services while reducing corporate costs and improving productivity’. Presumably reflecting its centrality to the programme, productivity is mentioned 39 times in the document.
key_recommendations: The Spending Review published alongside the 2026-27 Budget commits the Scottish government to a programme of reform ‘designed to protect frontline services while reducing corporate costs and improving productivity’.

Indeed, political discourse often seems to imply that easy and significant productivity gains in the delivery of Scotland’s public services are just waiting to be grasped if only the government could summon the requisite political will and managerial competence.
Baumol’s ‘cost disease’: why do the costs of delivering services such as health and education tend to increase at a rate above the whole economy rate of inflation?

Famously, Baumol uses examples from the performing arts to help illustrate the intrinsic difficulty of reducing labour inputs, and hence raising productivity, in the delivery of personal services: A half hour horn quintet calls for the expenditure of two and a half man hours in its performance, and any attempt to increase productivity here is likely to be viewed with concern by critics and audience alike.

recent_reports.title: Tradeable jobs and city centre regeneration: lessons from Wakefield
recent_reports.summary: Tradeable jobs and city centre regeneration: lessons from Wakefield | Centre for Cities Recently, Centre for Cities visited Wakefield. Alongside discovering the pivotal role the city plays in the Rhubarb Triangle , we learned about how the council is planning to develop the city centre into a place for more people to live and work.
key_recommendations: It was an increase in employment, not an increase in pay, that drove disposable income growth in Wakefield.

To raise wages and support the city centre, Wakefield is trying to attract in residents and businesses To support higher wages, the council is working to support more jobs in higher-paying, advanced manufacturing businesses.

By increasing the number of higher-qualified workers and providing new office space via developments like Tileyard North , the council is also hoping to attract knowledge-intensive businesses into the city centre to raise wages and provide even more daytime footfall.

With anchor retailers like Primark and M&S moving out , the council is going to use £17.9 million from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government to acquire the Ridings Shopping Centre, demolish it, and build 1,000 new homes in its place.

recent_reports.title: The Budget 2024 should commit to fiscal devolution

key_recommendations: The Budget 2024 should commit to fiscal devolution | Centre for Cities Ahead of Budget 2024, the public debate on tax and growth is heating up, and the hunt for rabbits is on.
While “how much”, “from who” and “what taxes” are important parts of this debate, the question of “which part of the state” is not getting nearly the attention it should.

Only five per cent of taxation in the UK in 2021 was collected by local government; below the 11 per cent average for non-federal OECD countries, and lower than other large non-federal states, such as 12 per cent in Poland; 14 per cent in France; 18 per cent in South Korea; and 23 per cent in Japan.
Before 1988, the UK’s share of taxation collected by local government was no different from the OECD non-federal average.

recent_reports.summary: The concentration of charities focused on local need in UK cities is limited both by the level and distribution of local incomes.
key_recommendations: But it is not just low income levels that reduce the number of these charities in UK cities.
First, an increase in the level of local income deprivation is associated with a decrease in the density of local needs-focused charities even when accounting for how it is distributed.
Third, an increase in the clustering of income deprivation is associated with a decrease in the charity density measure.

So to sustain voluntary organisations dedicated to meeting local economic need in the long term, national government must get the economies of left-behind cities firing again – Cities Outlook 2024 sets out the national steps to achieve local economic growth over the next decade.

recent_reports.title: Tech & DigitalisationTechnological Chokepoints: How to Balance Resilience and Leverage in a Weaponised EconomyPaper | 22nd April 2026Middle powers need a strategy to navigate technological interdependence: build resilience where it counts and use leverage wisely to stay competitive.
recent_reports.summary: It is not possible for leaders to opt out of the technological revolution. Yet, as well as a source of growth, technology is also an arena for competition and conflict.
key_recommendations: There is therefore a paradox: being part of this interdependent technological economy is necessary for competitiveness, security and building state capacity but, for precisely that reason, it is also an unequivocal source of vulnerability that must be grappled with.

recent_reports.title: Levying up
recent_reports.summary: An effective skills system is more important now than ever. In the coming decades, we are likely to see a transformation in the labour market, driven by advances in technology including artificial intelligence. Estimates suggest that between 10 per cent and 30 per cent of UK jobs have the potential to be automated in the coming years, with many more being transformed by technology.
key_recommendations: The levy is also failing to deliver on two of the government’s central missions: driving growth and unlocking opportunity.
The Labour government has committed to reforming the levy into a ‘growth and skills levy’, giving employers more flexibility.

In this report, general secretary Joe Dromey and senior researcher Sasjkia Otto set out a series of recommendations for the reform of the levy designed to both unleash growth and to unlock opportunity.
A decade ago, the Conservative government announced the introduction of the apprenticeship levy.

recent_reports.title: The UK's Broken Housing Market: Causes, Consequences and Cures
recent_reports.summary: Comprehensive diagnosis of UK housing dysfunction. Argues housing affordability crisis is 'the very core of the crisis of confidence in capitalism itself.' Sets out 16 specific reform recommendations focused on planning reform, land release, and property tax restructuring.
key_recommendations: Scrap the 1947 Town and Country Planning Act on a limited basis via a Special Development Order.
Introduce a new rules-based planning system based on zoning — trialled first in cities and their immediate environs.
Overhaul Green Belt designation: land of genuine environmental value recategorised as AONB; remaining land zoned for permitted development.
Reform council tax: introduce two additional bands at the top, one new band at the bottom; increase rates in top bands.
Introduce a Stamp Duty exemption for last-time buyers to encourage downsizing.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: Partial — Policy Exchange and Fudge agree on planning reform urgency and supply-side diagnosis. Fudge goes further with Land Value Tax; Policy Exchange focuses on council tax reform and zoning rather than LVT.

recent_reports.title: Homes for Growth
recent_reports.summary: Examines the macroeconomic consequences of housing undersupply. Argues housing shortage has a 'chilling effect on the economy as a whole.' Documents how wealth inequality driven by property is suppressing consumer spending — capital is being transferred from high-propensity-to-consume households to low-propensity-to-consume landlords. Housing benefit costs (£31.3bn projected 2025-26) will continue rising without structural supply reform.
key_recommendations: Housing supply is the central economic constraint on UK growth — must be treated as a macroeconomic priority, not just a social policy.
Wealth inequality driven by housing is non-neutral: it transfers spending power from renters to landlords, suppressing domestic demand.
Social housing waiting list of 1.19 million (2021) and 86,000 households in temporary accommodation represent both a human and fiscal crisis.
Growth requires housing — the two policy areas cannot be separated.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: High — directly supports Fudge's housing theory of everything thesis. Policy Exchange reaches similar conclusions from a centre-right supply-side perspective, without the LVT mechanism.

recent_reports.title: Pro-Growth Reforms Could Add Over £400bn to UK GDP
recent_reports.summary: Models the GDP impact of a suite of supply-side reforms across housing, energy, taxation, and regulation. Central estimate: 10–20% uplift to UK GDP over the long term, equivalent to £428bn additional GDP by 2036, or £5,800 per capita in 2036 nominal terms. Housing, energy costs, excessive taxation, and excessive regulation are the four binding constraints on UK growth. Co-published with the Adam Smith Institute.
key_recommendations: Planning reform alone could unlock significant GDP gains through improved capital deepening and labour mobility.
Private sector-led growth through deregulation and tax reform is the primary lever — not state investment.
UK faces an unprecedented growth challenge: current 1–2% forecasts are insufficient to sustain world-class public services.
Housing, energy costs, excessive taxation, and excessive regulation are the four binding constraints on UK growth.
recent_reports.hf_alignment_note: Partial — GDP uplift figures are in similar range to Fudge's +5.7% Y10 estimate, but mechanism differs fundamentally. Policy Exchange/ASI favour deregulation and private sector; Fudge favours public investment and industrial strategy alongside supply-side reform.
